lessons.title: The Skeletal System: Bones and Functions

knowledge_checks.q: Which two bones form the shoulder joint?
Which function of the skeleton is responsible for producing red blood cells?
The _____ sits in front of the knee joint and protects it.
OCR names _____ as a separate sixth function of the skeleton, distinct from support.
Match each bone group to its location in the body:

before.content_html:
The Framework of Movement

The human skeleton is a living structure made of 206 bones that provides the framework for every movement you make in sport. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against. The skeleton works in partnership with the muscular system: muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints. Understanding which bones are where — and what they do — underpins everything else in PE.

Bones of the Skeleton: Head to Toe

Working from the top of the body downwards, the cranium sits at the very top of the head, curving down around the brain. Below it, the vertebrae form a column of 33 bones running from the base of the skull to the pelvis — protecting the spinal cord and giving the trunk both stability and a controlled range of movement. At the front of the chest, the sternum (breastbone) and the ribs form the ribcage, encasing the heart and lungs. The clavicle (collarbone) connects the sternum to the shoulder on each side, and the flat, triangular scapula (shoulder blade) lies across the upper back.

The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Together, the scapula and humerus form the shoulder joint — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the body. At the elbow, three bones meet: the humerus, the radius (which runs along the thumb side of the forearm) and the ulna (which runs along the little-finger side). In the wrist and hand, the carpals form the wrist, the metacarpals form the palm, and the phalanges are the finger bones. These hand bones are named explicitly in the OCR specification and are examined directly — learn all three.

Moving to the lower body, the pelvis is a large basin-shaped structure at the base of the spine. It forms the hip joint with the head of the femur — a ball-and-socket joint allowing the greatest range of movement in the lower limb. At the knee, the femur articulates with the tibia (the large shin bone), forming a hinge joint. The patella sits in front of the knee joint. The fibula runs alongside the tibia on the outer side of the lower leg. At the foot, the tarsals form the ankle and heel, the metatarsals form the arch of the foot, and the phalanges are the toe bones — mirroring the hand structure.

Key Fact

OCR’s 19 named bones: cranium, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, clavicle, scapula, pelvis, humerus, ulna, radius, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals. The hand and foot bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, tarsals, metatarsals) are OCR-specific additions — make sure you can name and locate all of them.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton does far more than hold the body upright. It serves six distinct functions, each of which can be applied directly to sport and physical activity.

Support — the skeleton holds the body upright against gravity. A sprinter’s lower limbs support their entire body weight as they drive off the blocks. Without a rigid skeletal frame, the muscular system would have nothing to act on.

Posture — the vertebral column and pelvis maintain the upright alignment of the body. Good posture keeps the skeleton in correct mechanical alignment, reducing injury risk and allowing muscles to work most efficiently. A rower must maintain an upright spine throughout the drive phase; poor posture transfers force inefficiently and risks back injury. OCR lists posture as a distinct function, separate from support — always treat them as two separate marks.

Protection — flat bones protect vital organs. The cranium shields the brain; the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs. In contact sports such as rugby, the ribcage absorbs impact forces that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs directly.

Movement — bones act as levers. When the biceps contracts during a bicep curl, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) pivot at the elbow to lift the load. In kicking a football, the femur swings at the hip and the tibia swings at the knee, producing explosive leg extension.

Blood cell production — red bone marrow inside flat and irregular bones produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles during exercise via haemoglobin. This function links directly to cardiovascular performance: a well-functioning skeletal system supports oxygen delivery to muscles.

Storage of minerals — bones store calcium and phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when the body needs them, and weight-bearing exercise stimulates the bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production and storage of minerals. Each one links to sporting performance — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement), the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection), and the vertebral column maintains alignment during a rowing drive (posture).

A very common error is to list only five functions and miss posture entirely, or to treat posture and support as the same thing. In OCR, they are explicitly two separate functions. Support is about bearing the weight of the body against gravity — the skeleton stops you collapsing. Posture is about maintaining correct alignment and shape during movement — the spine and pelvis keep the body in the optimal mechanical position for efficient performance and injury prevention. In an exam, if you write “support/posture” as one combined answer, you will likely receive credit for only one function. Always list them separately and give a different sporting example for each.

OCR explicitly requires students to name and locate the carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), tarsals and metatarsals in addition to the major long bones. These bones matter in sport: the carpals and metacarpals absorb force during a gymnast’s handstand or a goalkeeper’s diving save; the metatarsals and tarsals form the arch of the foot, which distributes body weight during running and jumping. A question asking “name the bones of the hand” expects all three groups: carpals (wrist), metacarpals (palm) and phalanges (fingers).

lessons.title: Synovial Joints and Movement at Joints

before.content_html:
What Is a Synovial Joint?

Every freely movable joint in the body — at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee — is a synovial joint. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body, and they all share the same basic structure: a capsule surrounding the joint, fluid inside to reduce friction, and a range of soft-tissue structures that hold the joint together and prevent injury. Understanding these structures is important not just for anatomy, but for explaining how joints withstand the demands of sport.

Structures of a Synovial Joint

The outer shell of a synovial joint is the joint capsule. It is made of tough, fibrous connective tissue that wraps completely around the joint, holding the bones in position and containing the joint fluid. Inside the capsule, the synovial membrane lines the inner surface and produces synovial fluid — a viscous substance that coats the ends of the bones inside the joint, dramatically reducing friction and allowing bones to glide smoothly past each other. During the warm-up phase of exercise, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and spreads more effectively, which is one reason why warming up reduces injury risk.

Covering the ends of the bones inside the joint is articular cartilage, a smooth tissue that absorbs compressive forces and provides an almost frictionless surface. Ligaments are short, tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect bone to bone across the joint — the primary restraints against excessive movement. Tendons connect muscles to bone, transmitting contractile force to the skeleton to produce movement at the joint.

Key Fact

The four key components of a synovial joint: synovial fluid (lubricates and reduces friction between bone surfaces), articular cartilage (absorbs compression, provides frictionless surface), ligaments (connect bone to bone, prevent excessive movement), tendons (connect muscle to bone, transmit force for movement).

Types of Synovial Joint

OCR identifies two types of synovial joint and four specific joints that are directly examined. A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only — flexion and extension. The knee (femur articulating with the tibia) and the elbow (humerus articulating with the radius and ulna) are both hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in multiple planes. The shoulder (head of the humerus fitting into the socket of the scapula) and the hip (head of the femur fitting into the socket of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints.

Articulating Bones at Each Joint

The OCR specification requires you to name the articulating bones at all four joints. At the knee, the femur (thigh bone) articulates with the tibia (shin bone) — these two long bones form the hinge. At the elbow, the humerus articulates with both the radius and the ulna — three bones meet here, which is why the elbow allows both hinge movement (flexion/extension) and some rotation. At the shoulder, the humerus articulates with the scapula — the rounded head of the humerus sits in the shallow socket of the scapula, enabling the greatest range of movement in the body. At the hip, the femur articulates with the pelvis — the rounded head of the femur slots into the deep cup of the pelvis, creating a stable but mobile ball-and-socket joint.

Key Fact

Knee: femur + tibia (hinge). Elbow: humerus + radius + ulna (hinge). Shoulder: humerus + scapula (ball-and-socket). Hip: femur + pelvis (ball-and-socket). These are the four joints on the OCR specification — learn the articulating bones for each.

Types of Movement at Joints

Flexion is a decrease in the angle at a joint — bending. Extension is an increase in the angle — straightening. Both occur at all four OCR joints. At the elbow and knee (hinge joints), flexion and extension are the only movements possible because the structure of the joint restricts movement to a single plane.

At the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket joints), a much wider range of movements is available. Abduction is movement of a limb away from the midline — lifting the arm out to the side in a star jump. Adduction is movement towards the midline — bringing the arm back down. Both abduction and adduction are available at the shoulder and hip but not at the elbow or knee.

Rotation of the shoulder is turning the arm in or out along its long axis. A cricket bowler’s arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery. Circumduction of the shoulder is a circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the arm traces a full cone shape. Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.

A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); articular cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.

As body temperature rises during a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and distributes more evenly across the joint surfaces. This increases the range of movement available and reduces friction, meaning joints can work more efficiently. Ligaments and tendons also become more pliable at higher temperatures, reducing the risk of tears. This is the physiological reason why a warm-up includes a pulse raiser and stretching before high-intensity work.

Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. OCR also requires knowledge of a third muscle role — the fixator — which stabilises a nearby joint while movement occurs at another.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The trapezius is the large, diamond-shaped muscle that runs from the base of the skull down to the middle of the back. It elevates the shoulders, pulls the scapula back and assists head movement. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the broad muscle of the lower and mid-back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder — powerful in swimming backstroke and rowing movements. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the press-up or front crawl pull phase.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting and shortening to pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder throughout the bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow moves.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser and fixator.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping.

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping.

Key Fact

In the upward phase of a bicep curl: biceps = agonist (prime mover, contracts to flex the elbow), triceps = antagonist (relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), deltoid = fixator (stabilises the shoulder joint so the upper arm stays still). In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist.

Key Fact

The human body contains over 600 named muscles. Muscle fibres are packed with mitochondria — the organelles that produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying the energy needed for sustained muscular contraction during sport and exercise.

OCR explicitly requires three muscle roles — agonist, antagonist and fixator — while other boards only require two. Students who name only the agonist and antagonist will miss the fixator marks in OCR questions. A fixator is a muscle that holds a nearby body part still so that the prime mover can work efficiently. It does not produce the movement; it provides the stable base from which the movement occurs. In the bicep curl, the deltoid stabilises the shoulder joint throughout the exercise — without it, the shoulder would move and the elbow flexion would be inefficient. Always include the fixator and name the joint it stabilises.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist and fixator. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), fixator named and its role described (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.”

before.exam_tip_html: For a ‘Describe’ question asking you to describe a lever system in a sporting example, always name all three components (fulcrum, load and effort) and identify which body part acts as each. The fulcrum is always the joint — a common error is labelling the muscle itself as the fulcrum. On the 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ question about lever systems, make sure you evaluate both sides: what advantages does a particular lever system bring to performance, and what are its limitations? For example, third class levers (elbow in a throw) allow great speed but require significant muscular effort. A balanced answer anchors each point to a named sporting action. OCR only requires the definition of mechanical advantage, not a calculation — express it as “greater than 1” or “less than 1” and explain what that means for force or speed.

practice_questions.text: A school PE teacher argues that the body's reliance on third class levers in throwing and striking puts athletes at a mechanical disadvantage. Evaluate this view, considering the performance benefits and limitations of third class levers in sport compared with second class levers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of both lever classes; multiple sporting examples applied accurately; candidate clearly explains that third class levers do produce a mechanical disadvantage (effort arm shorter than load arm, MA less than 1, muscles must exert greater force than the load) but that this disadvantage is compensated by amplification of speed and range of movement; explains that second class levers (ankle in a calf raise) amplify force (MA greater than 1) but at the cost of speed; evaluates why the body needs both types for different functions; reaches a balanced conclusion acknowledging that ‘disadvantage’ is context-dependent — in striking and throwing sports, speed at the end of the limb is the goal, so third class levers are optimal for those tasks.

Secure: Both lever classes discussed with sporting examples; mostly accurate mechanical advantage explanations; conclusion reached; some balance in the argument.

Developing: One lever class discussed more thoroughly; limited comparison; sporting examples present but may not be precisely anchored to the body location.

Emerging: Basic description of lever classes; minimal evaluation of mechanical advantage or sporting application.

Agreeing with the teacher: third class levers (elbow in bicep curl, throwing action) do require the muscle to exert force greater than the load; MA less than 1 is technically a mechanical disadvantage; greater muscular effort is needed compared with a second class lever producing the same outcome.

Disagreeing / qualification: the ‘disadvantage’ in force production is traded for speed and range at the end of the limb; a javelin thrower’s hand speed is what determines throw distance — a second class lever at the elbow would produce greater force but far less speed; third class levers dominate the body because speed and range outweigh force requirements in most striking, catching and throwing sports; both lever types are essential — the ankle’s second class lever provides the force to drive the whole body off the ground; the elbow’s third class lever provides the speed to deliver a fast punch or throw.

before.content_html:
What Is a Lever System?

The human body is a machine built from levers. Every time you nod your head, rise onto your toes, or perform a bicep curl, you are using a lever system to transmit force. Understanding how levers work allows coaches and athletes to explain why some movements generate great force, and why others allow great speed but require more effort. A lever consists of three components arranged around a pivot point. The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point — in the body, a joint. The load (also called the resistance) is the weight or force being moved. The effort is the force applied to move that load — in the body, this is the force produced by the contracting muscle. The three classes of lever differ in the relative positions of these three components: fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E).

Key Fact

OCR pins each lever class to a specific body location: 1st class = neck (nodding the head), 2nd class = ankle (calf raise / plantar flexion), 3rd class = elbow (bicep curl). Learn these three locations — they are the examples OCR examines directly.

First Class Levers

In a first class lever, the fulcrum sits between the load and the effort. Think of a seesaw: the pivot is in the middle, with weight on one side and the pushing force on the other. In the body, the OCR example is the nodding action of the head at the neck: the skull (load) rests at one end, the neck extensor muscles (effort) pull from behind, and the atlantooccipital joint (fulcrum) sits between them. First class levers can produce both force and speed depending on where the effort and load arms fall relative to the fulcrum.

Second Class Levers

In a second class lever, the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. The classic everyday example is a wheelbarrow. In the body, the OCR example is plantar flexion at the ankle — rising onto the toes (a calf raise): the ball of the foot acts as the fulcrum at one end, the body weight (load) acts through the ankle joint in the middle, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (effort) pull via the Achilles tendon at the heel. The effort arm is longer than the load arm, so a relatively small muscular effort can move a larger load. Second class levers therefore produce a mechanical advantage greater than 1, making them excellent for force production.

Third Class Levers

In a third class lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. This is the most common lever arrangement in the human body. The OCR example is elbow flexion during a bicep curl: the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps apply effort just below the joint, and the load (the forearm, hand and any weight held) is at the far end. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so more muscular effort is needed to move the load. However, a small movement of the biceps produces a large movement of the hand — trading mechanical disadvantage for speed and range of movement. Third class levers therefore favour speed and range over force, which is why most striking and throwing actions in sport use them.

A very common exam error is mis-labelling the positions of the fulcrum, load and effort, or confusing which class a sporting example belongs to. A reliable approach is to identify the joint first (that is always the fulcrum), then identify what is being moved (the load, usually the body part or any weight), and finally identify where the muscle pulls (the effort). Once you have these three pinned, the class follows logically: if the joint (F) is in the middle, it is first class; if the weight (L) is in the middle, it is second class; if the muscle pull (E) is in the middle, it is third class. Anchor your answer to OCR’s three named body locations: neck (1st), ankle (2nd), elbow (3rd).

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage is a number that tells you whether a lever amplifies force or amplifies speed and range of movement. It compares the length of the effort arm (the distance from the fulcrum to where the effort is applied) with the length of the load arm (the distance from the fulcrum to where the load acts).

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the effort arm is longer than the load arm — a small effort produces a large force. This is the case in second class levers: rising onto the toes lifts your entire body weight with relatively modest calf muscle effort. A mechanical advantage less than 1 means the load arm is longer than the effort arm — more muscular effort is required, but the trade-off is greater speed and range. Third class levers have MA less than 1 — that is why bicep curls, throwing and striking actions require significant muscular effort but produce fast, wide movements at the end of the limb.

Unlike some other exam boards, OCR only requires you to know the definition of mechanical advantage — not to calculate it. You need to be able to explain what mechanical advantage means and state whether a given lever has an advantage greater than or less than 1. A good exam answer on mechanical advantage will: (1) state whether the effort arm or load arm is longer, (2) say whether this gives a MA greater than or less than 1, and (3) explain what that means for force production or speed. For example: “At the ankle during a calf raise, the effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) is longer than the load arm (heel to ankle joint), so the lever has a mechanical advantage greater than 1, meaning the calf muscles produce more force than the load they are lifting.”

Key Fact

Mechanical advantage greater than 1 = force is amplified (second class lever, e.g. ankle during a calf raise). Mechanical advantage less than 1 = speed and range of movement are amplified (most third class levers, e.g. elbow during a bicep curl). First class levers can have MA either above or below 1 depending on the relative positions of the fulcrum, load and effort.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System and Pathway of Blood

before.exam_tip_html: The cardiac output calculation is one of the most predictable questions in this topic — always worth attempting. Show three things: (1) the formula (Q = stroke volume × heart rate), (2) the substitution with figures from the question, and (3) the answer with the correct unit (ml/min or L/min). Missing the unit is a frequent error that costs the final mark. On a ‘Describe the pathway of blood’ question, a common mistake is to say the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood — it is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. OCR also requires you to name the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves and place them correctly in the blood pathway — not just state that “valves prevent backflow.” For the 8-mark Evaluate question, ensure your argument covers both sides: address what happens when the cardiovascular system functions efficiently and consider what happens when it is under stress, linking both to the specific sporting context given.

practice_questions.text: Name the vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: pulmonary vein.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cardiac output'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying cardiac output as the total volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute; 1 mark for stating it is calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate (or giving the formula Q = SV × HR).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows data for a trained cyclist at rest and during a 20-minute time trial.

Condition      | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
At rest        | 48               | 85
During race    | 172              | 115

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the time trial. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output with working shown: Q = 48 × 85 = 4,080 ml/min; 1 mark for correct exercise cardiac output with working shown: Q = 172 × 115 = 19,780 ml/min; 1 mark for including correct units (ml/min or equivalent L/min) on both answers. If method is correct but arithmetic is wrong, award 1 mark for the correct formula and substitution.

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old club swimmer's heart rate data is recorded during a training set. Resting: 62 bpm. End of warm-up: 105 bpm. Peak (mid-set): 178 bpm. Five minutes after finishing: 88 bpm.

Interpret what the data tells you about how the cardiovascular system responds during and after the swim set.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the increase in heart rate from rest to peak (116 bpm rise) and stating that this reflects the increased demand for oxygen from the working muscles; 1 mark for explaining that stroke volume also increases during exercise, meaning cardiac output rises substantially; 1 mark for identifying the recovery drop (from 178 bpm to 88 bpm within 5 minutes) and linking this to the body's return towards its resting state; 1 mark for a valid sporting interpretation (e.g. the large rise in heart rate confirms the high oxygen demand of competitive swimming; the drop in recovery heart rate suggests the swimmer is reasonably well conditioned). If calculations are used, show working and units.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves in the pathway of blood through the heart.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining the tricuspid valve: located between the right atrium and right ventricle; prevents blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium; 1 mark for explaining the bicuspid valve: located between the left atrium and left ventricle; prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium; 1 mark for explaining the semilunar valves: located at the exit of each ventricle (into the aorta and pulmonary artery); prevent backflow into the ventricles between beats; 1 mark for correctly placing all three in the sequence of blood flow through the heart. Accept equivalent anatomical descriptions.

practice_questions.text: A county-level middle-distance runner is preparing for a 12-week pre-season training block. Evaluate the importance of an efficient cardiovascular system to her performance in a competitive 800 m race, considering both heart structure and the pathway of blood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full range of relevant cardiovascular content applied consistently to 800 m racing. Includes: double-circulatory system (pulmonary and systemic loops) enabling continuous oxygen delivery; named valves preventing backflow ensuring one-directional flow; cardiac output calculation linked to exercise demand (heart rate and stroke volume both rising during the race); red blood cells transporting oxygen to the quadriceps and gastrocnemius during the race effort; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; long-term training adaptations (cardiac hypertrophy, increased stroke volume, lower resting heart rate) that improve efficiency. Evaluation includes both sides: the value of a highly efficient cardiovascular system vs the constraints (genetic ceiling on maximum cardiac output; lactic acid accumulation in the final stages regardless of cardiovascular fitness). Justified conclusion about whether cardiovascular efficiency is the most important limiting factor for 800 m performance. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most cardiovascular structures and responses covered with reasonable accuracy; applied to the 800 m context; evaluation of at least two relevant points; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped sections.

Developing (3-4 marks): Cardiovascular structures described with limited application to the 800 m race; cardiac output mentioned but not calculated or applied; one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about heart rate increasing during exercise; limited structure or sporting application.

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange

before.content_html:
The Journey Air Takes Into Your Body

Every time you inhale, air travels along a precisely ordered pathway before oxygen reaches your working muscles. Understanding this route is essential for explaining how the body meets the increased demand for oxygen during exercise. Air enters through the mouth or nose, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered. It then passes into the trachea — the windpipe — which is kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. From the trachea, air divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), one entering each lung. Inside the lungs, the bronchi branch repeatedly into smaller and smaller tubes called bronchioles. The bronchioles finally open out into tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus), and it is here that the vital process of gas exchange occurs.

Key Fact

The pathway of air follows six stages in sequence: mouth/nose → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. OCR specifically includes both mouth and nose at the start of the pathway. Commit this order to memory — it appears regularly in short-answer questions.

Gaseous Exchange at the Alveoli

Gaseous exchange is the movement of gases between the lungs and the bloodstream. It relies on diffusion — molecules naturally move from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. In the alveoli, the concentration of oxygen is high (freshly inhaled air) while the blood arriving from the body has a low oxygen concentration and a high concentration of carbon dioxide. As a result, oxygen diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, out of the blood and into the alveolus to be exhaled.

Six structural features of the alveoli are specifically designed to maximise the speed and efficiency of this exchange. First, the alveoli have a very large surface area in total — hundreds of millions of tiny sacs create an enormous surface for diffusion to occur across. Second, the alveolar walls are moist and only one cell thick, meaning the distance gases must travel is as short as possible. Third, the alveoli are surrounded by a rich network of capillaries, ensuring a continuous and large blood supply. Fourth, blood flowing through these capillaries is constantly replenished (deoxygenated blood arrives and oxygenated blood leaves), which maintains the concentration gradient that drives diffusion.

Once oxygen crosses into the blood, it binds with haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. This oxygenated blood then travels via the pulmonary veins to the left side of the heart and is pumped out to the working muscles. Haemoglobin can also carry carbon dioxide on the return journey to the lungs.

A common misunderstanding is that oxygen delivery to muscles is purely about breathing harder. In fact, the rate of diffusion at the alveoli is limited by concentration gradients and surface area — you cannot increase the surface area of your alveoli by trying harder. What exercise does achieve is an increased breathing rate and deeper breaths (greater tidal volume), which refreshes the air in the alveoli more frequently, maintaining a strong concentration gradient. Additionally, more capillaries open up around active alveoli during exercise, increasing the effective surface area available for gas exchange. The structural adaptations of the alveoli — thin walls, large surface area, rich blood supply — are what make rapid exchange possible, not effort alone.

The Mechanics of Breathing

Breathing is an active mechanical process driven by muscles changing the volume and pressure inside the chest cavity. During inhalation at rest, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, while the intercostal muscles contract to raise the rib cage upward and outward. These combined actions increase the volume of the chest cavity, which lowers the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure. Air rushes in from outside to equalise the pressure — this is inhalation. During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax. The rib cage falls inward and downward under gravity, reducing the chest volume and increasing pressure in the lungs. Air is pushed out passively. Breathing at rest is therefore largely passive on the exhale.

During intense exercise, the body must move air much more forcefully and rapidly. On the inhale, accessory muscles come into play: the pectorals (chest muscles) help to elevate the rib cage further and faster. On the exhale, the abdominal muscles actively contract, pulling the rib cage down more quickly and forcefully expelling air. This ensures that stale air (rich in carbon dioxide) is cleared from the lungs faster, making room for fresh, oxygen-rich air.

Breathing Rate, Tidal Volume and Minute Ventilation

Breathing rate is the number of breaths taken per minute. At rest, a typical breathing rate is around 12–15 breaths per minute. During maximal exercise this can rise to 40–60 breaths per minute. Note that OCR uses the term “breathing rate” — not “respiratory rate.”

Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in or out with each breath. At rest, tidal volume is approximately 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise it can rise to 3 litres or more as the body draws on its deeper breath capacity.

Minute ventilation is the total volume of air moved per minute and equals tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate. For example, a resting athlete breathing at 15 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.5 litres has a minute ventilation of 7.5 litres per minute. During hard exercise, both tidal volume and breathing rate increase, so minute ventilation can rise to 100–150 litres per minute in trained performers. This enormous increase ensures the concentration gradient at the alveoli is maintained even as muscles consume oxygen at a high rate.

Key Fact

Six features make alveolar gas exchange efficient: large surface area, moist thin walls (one cell thick), short diffusion distance, large capillary network, large blood supply, and a maintained concentration gradient (high O2 in alveoli, low CO2 in arriving blood).

Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate. Always show the formula and include the unit (litres per minute or L/min). Example at rest: 0.5 L × 15 breaths/min = 7.5 L/min. Example during exercise: 2.5 L × 40 breaths/min = 100 L/min. A common error is using “respiratory rate” instead of “breathing rate” — OCR specifies breathing rate. Also make sure you do not confuse tidal volume (per breath) with minute ventilation (per minute).
before.exam_tip_html: For “describe” questions on gaseous exchange, students often say oxygen “moves into the blood” without explaining why — the mark scheme almost always requires the word “diffusion” and a reference to the concentration gradient (high to low). For “state two” questions on respiratory muscles, do not give the same answer twice — naming both the diaphragm and intercostals is required; stating just “the breathing muscles” twice earns only one mark. For 6-mark “analyse” questions, go beyond description: link each structural feature of the alveolus to a specific sporting implication. For example, “the large surface area of the alveoli means a marathon runner can exchange sufficient oxygen even at race pace, sustaining aerobic energy production.” Bullet-point responses rarely score above the Developing band — extended-response questions reward connected prose where each point is developed with a sporting example. Always use the OCR term “breathing rate” not “respiratory rate.”

glossary_terms.definition: The windpipe; a rigid tube reinforced with C-shaped rings of cartilage that carries air from the larynx down to the bronchi.
The two main branches of the airway that divide from the trachea and enter each lung.
The smallest air-conducting tubes within the lung, leading air from the bronchi to the alveoli.
Microscopic air sacs at the end of the bronchioles where gas exchange between air and blood takes place.
The process by which oxygen and carbon dioxide move between the alveoli and the blood in surrounding capillaries, driven by differences in concentration.
The movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, requiring no energy.
The red protein inside red blood cells that combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin and transports it around the body.
The dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs that contracts and flattens during inhalation, increasing the vertical space in the chest cavity.
The muscles between the ribs (external and internal intercostals) that raise and lower the rib cage to assist breathing.
The number of breaths taken per minute (the OCR-specified term; not 'respiratory rate').
The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single breath during normal breathing.
The total volume of air breathed in or out per minute, calculated as tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate.

before.exam_tip_html: For “identify” and shorter questions on aerobic vs anaerobic, a common error is giving the activity name without any justification. Even a 1-mark question may expect you to say why: “anaerobic, because the high intensity means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, students often produce one-sided answers that only describe the positive features of aerobic exercise without considering trade-offs, or vice versa. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Build your response using a “For X… However Y…” structure, anchor each point to a named sport or athlete type, and end with a justified conclusion. Also note: OCR does not require you to define or use the terms EPOC, oxygen debt or DOMS at this level — focus on the definitions, word equations and the intensity-duration justification.

practice_questions.text: Identify whether the following activity is aerobic or anaerobic: a swimmer completing a 200 m race at maximum effort in approximately 2 minutes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anaerobic (or predominantly anaerobic). The very high intensity over approximately 2 minutes means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough. Accept: anaerobic exercise / uses the anaerobic pathway. Do not accept 'aerobic' for full credit.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'anaerobic exercise'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that anaerobic exercise takes place without sufficient oxygen; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down to produce energy and lactic acid as a by-product.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct differences: aerobic uses oxygen / anaerobic does not use sufficient oxygen; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water / anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic can be sustained for longer / anaerobic is short duration; aerobic is lower intensity / anaerobic is very high intensity. Do not award two marks for the same physiological point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text: A county-level basketball player performs a 30-second burst of high-intensity court sprints and jumps during a training drill. Describe why lactic acid accumulates during this effort and what effect this has on the player.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the exercise intensity is too high for oxygen to be delivered fast enough, triggering anaerobic respiration; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product; 1 mark for describing the consequence (lactic acid accumulates in the muscles and blood, causing fatigue and a burning sensation, limiting the player's ability to sustain the effort).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a 100 m sprinter and a 5,000 m runner require training for different energy systems, even though both are performing running events.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining that the 100 m sprint (approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity) is predominantly anaerobic because the energy demand rate exceeds oxygen delivery capacity; 1 mark for stating the word equation for anaerobic respiration (glucose → energy + lactic acid); 1 mark for explaining that the 5,000 m (13+ minutes at sustained high intensity) is predominantly aerobic because oxygen delivery can keep pace with demand over the longer duration; 1 mark for stating the word equation for aerobic respiration (glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water) and linking to the sustained effort the aerobic system allows.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level hockey player competes in a 70-minute outdoor match. Evaluate which energy system — aerobic or anaerobic — is more important to her overall match performance, and how each contributes at different points in the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced, well-developed evaluation with consistent sporting application to hockey. Aerobic system: dominant during the majority of the match (jogging, sustained running, sustained press); defined correctly (glucose + oxygen → energy + CO2 + water); advantages — sustainable over 70 minutes, efficient energy production, supports cardiovascular endurance; supported by specific examples (maintaining pressing throughout the second half). Anaerobic system: dominant during explosive moments (sprinting to intercept a pass, penalty corner execution, tackling); defined correctly (glucose → energy + lactic acid); advantages — fast energy release for high-intensity bursts; limitations — lactic acid builds up, causes fatigue, cannot be sustained. Evaluation reaches a justified conclusion: aerobic system is more important overall due to the 70-minute duration, but anaerobic capacity determines performance in decisive moments. Both sides consistently anchored to hockey-specific examples.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both systems addressed with reasonable accuracy and applied to hockey; evaluation of both sides present; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped points.

Developing (3-4 marks): One system covered well, or both described with limited evaluation; sporting context present but limited; may not reach a clear conclusion.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic identification of aerobic or anaerobic with minimal development; little or no sporting application to hockey.

lessons.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise

before.exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about effects of exercise is confusing the two timescales. Short-term effects occur during or immediately after exercise — they are temporary. Long-term effects take months or years of consistent training to develop. In “describe” and “explain” questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy, which leads to a lower resting heart rate.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, go beyond listing: connect the adaptation to a named component of fitness and then to a sporting performance benefit. For example: “Capillarisation increases the density of capillaries in the quadriceps, improving oxygen delivery, which improves cardiovascular endurance and allows a county cyclist to sustain a higher pace over a 40 km time trial without fatigue.” The data-handling questions in this topic require you to quote a figure from the table, describe what it shows, and explain the sporting implication — all three steps are needed for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Identify one short-term effect of exercise on the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased stroke volume; increased cardiac output; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'capillarisation' as a long-term effect of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying capillarisation as the growth of new capillaries in and around trained muscle tissue; 1 mark for stating that this increases capillary density and improves oxygen delivery to the muscle fibres (or: improves the removal of waste products such as CO2).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows resting heart rate data for three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Amira   | 74                      | 59
Ben     | 70                      | 57
Chloe   | 76                      | 62

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Amira: 15 bpm; Ben: 13 bpm; Chloe: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (15 + 13 + 14 = 42 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 14 bpm (accept 14.0). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate and stroke volume data at rest and during a 10 km race for a trained distance runner.

Condition     | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
At rest       | 52               | 88
During race   | 185              | 118

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the race, and interpret what the data tells you about the runner's cardiovascular fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output: Q = 52 × 88 = 4,576 ml/min; 1 mark for correct race cardiac output: Q = 185 × 118 = 21,830 ml/min; 1 mark for a valid comparison (e.g. cardiac output increases approximately 4.8 times during the race compared with rest, from 4,576 to 21,830 ml/min); 1 mark for a sporting interpretation (e.g. the low resting heart rate of 52 bpm suggests long-term cardiac hypertrophy, with a high stroke volume of 88 ml at rest indicating an efficient, trained heart capable of meeting the greatly elevated oxygen demand during the 10 km). If calculations are incorrect but method is sound, award 1 mark for working and 1 mark for a valid interpretation of their figures.

practice_questions.text: Explain how hypertrophy of the heart leads to a lower resting heart rate in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining hypertrophy of the heart as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to regular training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming a lower resting heart rate as the result (accept: bradycardia; state that it is typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level netball player has been following a structured 8-month fitness programme. Evaluate the short-term and long-term effects this programme is likely to have had on her cardiovascular and respiratory systems, and explain how these effects could improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full range of short-term and long-term effects covered with accuracy. Short-term: increased heart rate/stroke volume/cardiac output during matches; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; increased breathing rate and tidal volume; increased oxygen delivery; lactic acid production during explosive efforts. Long-term: hypertrophy of the heart; lower resting heart rate (with mechanism explained); increased resting stroke volume and cardiac output; capillarisation improving oxygen delivery to muscles; stronger respiratory muscles; improved aerobic capacity; better rate of recovery; improved resistance to fatigue. Each adaptation linked to a specific netball performance benefit (e.g. capillarisation supports sustained running in attack/defence; lower resting heart rate means she recovers faster between high-intensity passages of play; stronger respiratory muscles support higher minute ventilation during intense defensive sets). Evaluation includes at least one limitation or counter-argument (e.g. long-term adaptations take months and are reversible if training stops; short-term fatigue can temporarily impair performance; genetic ceiling on cardiac output). Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most cardiovascular and respiratory effects covered with reasonable accuracy; most applied to netball; some evaluation; conclusion reached.

Developing (3-4 marks): Short-term or long-term effects described but not both; limited sporting application to netball; one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic reference to heart rate increasing during exercise or the heart getting bigger; limited application or evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a LONG-TERM effect of regular endurance training?
What does 'capillarisation' mean as a long-term effect of exercise?
options: The heart grows larger and stronger
Lactic acid is produced more efficiently
New capillaries grow in trained muscle tissue, increasing oxygen delivery

knowledge_checks.q: Redistribution of blood flow during exercise means more blood is directed towards _____ muscles.
An anticipatory rise in heart rate before exercise begins is triggered by the release of _____.
Match each effect of exercise to the correct timescale:
right: Short-term (during or after a single session)

lessons.title: Components of Fitness and Fitness Tests

before.exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to “define” a component of fitness, you must include the key elements of the definition: for example, cardiovascular endurance requires “heart and lungs” AND “sustained exercise” to earn both marks. On “explain” or “analyse” questions about components, you must name the component, define it briefly AND justify its relevance with a sporting example — three elements are expected. Simply listing components without explanation is a very common error that loses marks. For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, avoid saying “all components are important” — the question is asking you to discriminate, prioritise and justify with reasons. The data-interpretation questions in this topic may include a fabricated fitness test results table — always quote a specific figure, make a comparison, and link to a sporting performance implication.

practice_questions.text:
Which fitness test is used to measure cardiovascular endurance?
A) Illinois agility test
B) Stork stand test
C) Cooper 12-minute run
D) Sit and reach test
practice_questions.marks: C — Cooper 12-minute run. [1 mark] (Also accept: multi-stage fitness test, if both options were listed.)

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'agility'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying agility as the ability to change body position quickly; 1 mark for specifying accurately while moving (accept: with speed and control; quickly and accurately).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows vertical jump scores for four athletes before and after a 10-week plyometric training programme.

Athlete | Score before (cm) | Score after (cm)
Dan     | 38                | 45
Ellie   | 41                | 50
Fatima  | 36                | 43
George  | 44                | 52

Calculate the mean improvement in vertical jump score across all four athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual improvement (Dan: 7; Ellie: 9; Fatima: 7; George: 8); 1 mark for summing correctly (7 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 31) and dividing by 4; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 7.75 cm (accept 7.8 or 8 cm). Units required (cm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text:
A county-level badminton player wants to know which fitness tests are most relevant for measuring her sport-specific fitness. Interpret the data below and suggest which test results are most meaningful for her performance.

Test              | Result
Cooper run        | 2,450 m
Illinois agility  | 16.4 seconds
Vertical jump     | 42 cm
Ruler drop        | 18 cm

Explain which two results are most important for her and why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the Illinois agility test result (16.4 seconds) as most relevant, with a reason (badminton requires frequent direction changes to reach the shuttlecock across the court — agility is central to performance); 1 mark for identifying the ruler drop / reaction time (18 cm) as the second most important, with a reason (fast reaction time allows the player to respond to smashes and drops from the opponent before they can place the shuttlecock beyond her reach); 1 mark for quoting the specific figures from the table in the explanation; 1 mark for a valid evaluation of the other results (e.g. Cooper run is less critical than in endurance sports because rallies are short bursts; vertical jump is useful but not the primary performance-limiting factor in badminton).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gymnast competing on the balance beam requires balance and flexibility as two of their most important fitness components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining balance (the ability to retain the centre of mass over its base of support): the gymnast must maintain balance on a 10 cm-wide beam throughout their routine; 1 mark for applying balance to a named movement (e.g. holding a scale on one leg requires static balance); 1 mark for explaining flexibility (the range of movement possible at a joint): extreme joint mobility is needed to perform splits, walkovers and leaps to the required technical standard; 1 mark for applying flexibility to a named movement (e.g. a backbend walkover demands extreme spinal and hip flexibility to complete safely and score high artistic marks).

practice_questions.text: A PE teacher is designing a fitness testing programme for a Year-11 athletics squad. The squad includes 100 m sprinters and 1500 m runners. Evaluate which fitness components and tests are most important for each group, and whether any components are equally important for both.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full range of components covered for both event groups, each with precise definitions and named OCR tests. 100 m: reaction time (ruler drop — leaving the blocks immediately); power (vertical jump — explosive acceleration from blocks); speed (30 m sprint — maximum velocity during the race); muscular endurance (sustaining maximal effort for 10-12 seconds). 1500 m: cardiovascular endurance (Cooper run / multi-stage — sustained oxygen supply over 4+ minutes); muscular endurance (press-up/sit-up — repeated muscle contractions over several laps); speed (30 m sprint — finishing kick); flexibility (sit and reach — stride efficiency and injury prevention). Shared components: muscular endurance (both events require it, though for different durations and intensities); speed (both benefit from speed, though it is the primary goal only for sprinters). Evaluation addresses trade-offs: sprint testing (reaction time, power) would be irrelevant data for a distance runner's training programme; cardiovascular endurance testing is largely irrelevant for a 100 m sprinter. Justified conclusion about how component priorities differ by event and why the teacher should test selectively. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most components covered for both groups with accurate definitions; named tests included; comparison made; conclusion reached; some minor gaps.

Developing (3-4 marks): Components identified for one or both groups; limited test knowledge; some sporting application; one-sided or lacking comparison.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Names one or two components with minimal explanation; little or no reference to tests or evaluation.

before.content_html:
The Ten Components of Fitness

The specification identifies ten components of fitness. No single sport requires all ten in equal measure, so a key skill is identifying which components are most relevant to a given activity and justifying why. In OCR, component definitions and their standard fitness tests are examined together as a single topic — you must know both the definition of each component and the test used to measure it.

Cardiovascular endurance (also called stamina) is the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to the working muscles during sustained exercise. It is the foundation of performance in long-distance running, cycling, football and rowing. Tests: the Cooper 12-minute run (maximum distance covered in 12 minutes) and the multi-stage fitness test (bleep test — running between two lines 20 m apart in time with a beep that gets progressively faster).

Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle to undergo repeated contractions over a long period without tiring. Important in rowing, cycling and long-distance swimming. Tests: the press-up test (maximum press-ups in one minute) and the sit-up test (maximum sit-ups in one minute).

Speed is the maximum rate at which an individual is able to perform a movement or cover a distance in a period of time. Relevant in sprinting, a winger accelerating past a defender, or a serve in tennis. Test: the 30 m sprint test (time taken to sprint 30 m from a standing start).

Strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert against a resistance. Crucial in scrummaging in rugby, throwing events in athletics and weightlifting. Tests: the grip strength dynamometer test (maximum squeezing force measured in kg) and the 1 Repetition Maximum (1RM) (the heaviest single lift an athlete can perform with correct technique for a given exercise).

Power (also called explosive strength) is the ability to exert maximum force in as short a time as possible — it combines strength and speed. Critical in sprinting, shot-put, plyometric jumps and boxing combinations. Test: the vertical jump test (also called the standing jump test — maximum height of a standing jump, measured in cm).

Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. Crucial in gymnastics, dance, swimming (stroke efficiency) and martial arts. Test: the sit and reach test (reaching forward with straight legs from a seated position, measuring how far beyond the feet the fingers can reach).

Agility is the ability to change body position quickly and accurately while moving. Essential in team sports such as rugby, basketball and hockey where players must dodge opponents and change direction at speed. Test: the Illinois agility test (navigating a timed course with direction changes around cones).

Balance is the ability to retain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support. Can be static (holding a handstand) or dynamic (a gymnast on a balance beam). Important in gymnastics, surfing, skiing and judo. Test: the stork stand test (standing on one leg with the other foot resting against the knee, measuring how long balance can be maintained with eyes closed).

Coordination is the ability to use two or more body parts together smoothly and efficiently. Vital in cricket (eye-hand coordination for batting), tennis and swimming (synchronising arms and legs). Test: the wall throw test (throwing and catching a ball against a wall as many times as possible in 30 seconds, measuring the number of catches).

Reaction time is the time taken to initiate a response to a stimulus. A sprinter reacting to the starting gun, a goalkeeper responding to a shot, and a batsman reading a delivery all depend on a fast reaction time. Test: the ruler drop test (a ruler is dropped without warning and the participant catches it as fast as possible; the distance dropped in cm before it is caught indicates reaction time).

Key Fact

The ten components and their OCR-specified tests: cardiovascular endurance (Cooper 12-min run / multi-stage fitness test); muscular endurance (press-up / sit-up test); speed (30 m sprint); strength (grip dynamometer / 1RM); power (vertical jump); flexibility (sit and reach); agility (Illinois agility test); balance (stork stand); coordination (wall throw); reaction time (ruler drop test). Questions often ask you to select a component, define it AND name its test.

A very common exam error is naming a component without justifying why it matters for the specific sport in the question. Simply writing “cardiovascular endurance is important for football” will not earn full marks. The full answer should name the component, define it, and then give a sport-specific reason: “Cardiovascular endurance — the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to working muscles during sustained exercise — is important for a football midfielder because they must maintain high-intensity running across the full 90 minutes of a match.” Avoid saying “all components are important” — questions are testing your ability to discriminate and prioritise with reasons.

A 100 m sprinter needs: (1) reaction time — to leave the blocks the instant the starter’s pistol fires, reducing the overall race time; (2) power — to accelerate explosively from the blocks during the drive phase; (3) speed — to maintain maximum velocity during the top-speed phase; and (4) muscular endurance — to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10–12 seconds. Cardiovascular endurance is less important than in a marathon because the race duration is too short for the aerobic system to be the limiting factor. Always justify why the component matters for that specific sport — not just list its name.

Key Fact

OCR includes both the Cooper 12-minute run test and the multi-stage fitness test as valid tests for cardiovascular endurance. The Cooper test uses distance (metres) as the measure; the multi-stage test uses a level and shuttle number. Either is acceptable when asked to name a cardiovascular endurance test.

Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session causes the right adaptations without injury or wasted effort. Two frameworks summarise these principles: SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) and FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Together they provide a blueprint for designing any training programme, from a beginner’s fitness plan to an international athlete’s competition preparation.

SPOR: The Four Principles

Specificity — training must be designed to match the specific demands of the sport and the individual. A sprinter must train the fast-twitch muscle fibres and anaerobic energy systems used in a 100 m race; continuous low-intensity jogging would not develop the right adaptations. A swimmer should train in the water to develop sport-specific cardiovascular and muscular endurance rather than only running. If the training is not specific to the sport, the gains will not transfer to performance.

Progressive overload — the body adapts to the demands placed upon it. Once it has adapted, the same training stimulus produces no further improvement. To keep progressing, the training load must be gradually and continuously increased — using the FITT variables. A weight trainer who always lifts the same weight will plateau; they must add weight, more sets or more repetitions to continue building strength. The progression must be gradual: too-rapid increases lead to injury.

Reversibility — fitness adaptations are not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced — due to injury, illness or a long break — the body returns towards its pre-training state. Cardiovascular adaptations (such as a lower resting heart rate and larger stroke volume) reverse relatively quickly, often within a few weeks. Muscle mass is lost more slowly. This principle underlines why consistent, year-round training is more effective than intense bursts followed by long rest periods.

Recovery — sufficient rest must be built into any training programme. Without recovery time, the body cannot repair the microscopic muscle damage caused by training and cannot make the physiological adaptations that lead to improved fitness. Overtraining — training too hard without enough rest — leads to fatigue, declining performance and increased injury risk. Planning rest days or lower-intensity recovery sessions between hard efforts is as important as the training itself.

Key Fact

SPOR: Specificity (match training to sport demands), Progressive Overload (gradually increase load to keep adapting), Overload/reversibility (gains are lost if training stops — see Reversibility), Recovery (adequate rest allows the body to adapt). Note: OCR uses SPOR — Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery — not SPORT. There is no Tedium principle in OCR.

SPOR and FITT are complementary but distinct. SPOR gives the overarching principles — the “why” and “what” of training design (should training be specific? yes; should load progress? yes; must recovery be planned? yes). FITT gives the four variables you can actually manipulate to achieve those principles — the “how.” For example, applying progressive overload (a SPOR principle) is achieved by increasing frequency, intensity or time (all FITT variables). Understanding this relationship is often tested through questions asking you to “apply the FITT principles to achieve progressive overload for a specific athlete.”

FITT: The Four Training Variables

Frequency — how often a person trains per week. A beginner might train twice a week to allow full recovery; an elite endurance athlete may train twice a day. Frequency must be balanced against recovery: too many sessions without rest leads to overtraining and injury, too few limits adaptation.

Intensity — how hard the training is. Intensity can be expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate (for cardiovascular training), a percentage of one rep max (for weight training), or by effort level or speed. The aerobic training zone is 60–80% of maximum heart rate; the anaerobic zone is 80–90%. Choosing the right intensity ensures the correct energy system is stressed.

Time — the duration of a training session or individual exercise bout. A continuous run lasting 30 minutes will primarily stress the aerobic system; interval sprint sessions of 10 seconds each stress the anaerobic system.

Type — the method of training used. Type must align with the principle of specificity: a long-distance runner should use continuous training; a boxer should use circuit training with punching drills and HIIT; a gymnast needing flexibility should include stretching within a structured warm-up and cool-down. Choosing the wrong type of training may improve a general component of fitness without translating to sport-specific performance gains.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard — linked to training zones and heart rate %), Time (how long), Type (which training method). All four can be increased to apply progressive overload. Intensity links directly to training thresholds: aerobic 60–80% max HR; anaerobic 80–90% max HR.

A county-level 400 m freestyle swimmer applies the principles as follows. Specificity: all endurance sessions are in the pool using freestyle technique, not on a running track. Progressive overload: over 12 weeks the swimmer increases weekly distance by 10% and gradually shortens rest intervals between repetitions. Reversibility: during the off-season the swimmer maintains 50% of their training volume with twice-weekly pool sessions so that cardiovascular adaptations are not lost. Recovery: a complete rest day is built in after every two hard training days to allow muscle repair and adaptation. For FITT: frequency moves from 4 to 6 sessions per week over the training block; intensity is set at 70% of max HR for aerobic sets and 85% for higher-intensity sets; time per session increases from 60 to 90 minutes; type rotates between continuous, fartlek and interval training in the pool.

Applying SPOR and FITT Together

The most effective training programmes use both frameworks simultaneously. Specificity determines the training type; progressive overload is achieved by manipulating frequency, intensity and time over weeks and months; reversibility reminds the coach to maintain a training stimulus during breaks; and recovery ensures adequate rest is planned so the body can adapt. When you are asked to “design a training programme” or “evaluate the effectiveness of a training plan,” check whether all four SPOR principles and all four FITT variables are appropriately applied.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SPOR stands for Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility and Recovery — these are the overarching principles that should underpin any training programme. OCR does not include Tedium.
  • FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type — these are the four variables that can be adjusted to implement progressive overload and ensure specificity.
  • SPOR and FITT work together: SPOR explains why changes should be made; FITT explains how to make them in practice.
before.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sporting example. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progressive overload” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: OCR uses SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) — there is no Tedium principle. Confusing this with other boards’ acronyms is a common error.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): evaluates each SPOR principle with a two-sided argument. Progressive overload: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Recovery: in team sport, fixture schedules may not allow ideal recovery between matches, requiring careful management of training load in-season.
