Developing (3–4 marks): at least two SPOR principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.

before.content_html:
Why Warm Up and Cool Down?

Every training session and competitive performance should begin with a structured warm-up and end with a structured cool-down. These are not optional extras — they are physiologically grounded practices that reduce the risk of injury, improve performance quality during the session and accelerate recovery afterwards. OCR is more prescriptive than many boards: it names five specific components of a warm-up and lists eight distinct physical benefits. Knowing both lists precisely is essential.

The Five Components of a Warm-Up

OCR identifies five components in a structured warm-up. They should be delivered in this order, because each builds on the physiological preparation provided by the last.

The first component is a pulse raiser. This involves light aerobic activity — a gentle jog, dynamic movements or easy cycling — that gradually increases the heart rate, raises body temperature and begins redirecting blood flow towards the working muscles through vasodilation. The pace is deliberately modest at the start and builds progressively over several minutes. Starting a session with a flat sprint from cold would risk muscle strains because muscles are stiffer and less pliable at rest.

The second component is mobility exercises. These are controlled rotations and movements of the joints — neck rolls, shoulder circles, hip rotations, ankle circles — that take each joint through its range of motion without the additional challenge of increased load. Mobility work ensures synovial fluid is distributed throughout the joint capsule, making joints more fluid and reducing stiffness before greater demands are placed on them.

The third component is stretching. Dynamic stretching — such as leg swings, hip circles and shoulder rotations — is preferred during a warm-up because it maintains movement and keeps the heart rate elevated. The increased body temperature from the pulse raiser means the muscles are already more pliable, allowing a greater range of movement to be achieved safely.

The fourth component is dynamic movements. These are sport-specific exercises that begin to increase the intensity towards the demands of the activity — for example, lateral shuffles and change-of-direction runs for a netball player, or approach runs for a jumper. Dynamic movements challenge the neuromuscular system with patterns that closely resemble those required in competition, bridging the gap between general preparation and full effort.

The fifth component is skill rehearsal. This involves practising the actual skills of the sport at moderate intensity — a basketball team might include dribbling and shooting drills; a gymnast might rehearse scaled-down versions of her floor routines. Skill rehearsal ensures the neuromuscular system is primed for the precise movement patterns the sport requires and builds confidence before full competitive demands begin.

Key Fact

OCR’s five warm-up components in order: (1) pulse raiser — raises heart rate and body temperature; (2) mobility — loosens joints through their range of motion; (3) stretching — increases muscle pliability and range of movement; (4) dynamic movements — sport-specific exercises at increasing intensity; (5) skill rehearsal — rehearses the precise skills of the sport.

Physical Benefits of Warming Up

OCR lists eight specific physical benefits of a warm-up. Raising body temperature warms the muscles and preparing the body for physical activity so the muscle fibres become more pliable and less susceptible to strain. The elevated body temperature increases the speed at which nerve impulses travel, so the speed of muscle contraction improves — meaning athletes can move and react faster from the very first minutes of exercise.

Blood flow and oxygen delivery to the working muscles increases as cardiac output rises and blood is redirected away from the digestive organs towards the skeletal muscles. This ensures the aerobic energy system is ready to function efficiently from the start. Heart rate increases progressively, preparing the cardiovascular system for the demands ahead rather than shocking it into sudden high demand. Flexibility of muscles and joints improves as the temperature rise makes muscle fibres and surrounding connective tissue more elastic. The pliability of ligaments and tendons also increases with temperature, reducing the likelihood of tears and strains during explosive movements.

Recall from the cardiovascular and respiratory lessons that cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. During a warm-up, both stroke volume and heart rate begin to rise as the body prepares for activity. Blood is redistributed from the digestive organs towards the skeletal muscles through vasodilation in the muscle capillaries. Breathing rate and tidal volume also begin to rise, increasing the oxygen supply reaching the alveoli for gas exchange. A warm-up reinforces this anticipatory cardiovascular and respiratory response and continues the upward physiological response at a controlled pace, reducing the risk of the system being overwhelmed at the start of intense exercise.

The Components of a Cool-Down

After exercise, an immediate stop is physiologically harmful: blood can pool in the lower limbs when muscular contractions no longer pump it back towards the heart, causing dizziness and slowing the removal of waste products. A structured cool-down prevents this. OCR identifies two components: low intensity exercise and stretching.

The first component is low intensity exercise. Moving from a sprint to a jog, then from a jog to a brisk walk, then to a gentle stroll, keeps blood circulating so that lactic acid and carbon dioxide are transported to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal. This gradual decrease also avoids blood pooling in the limbs.

The second component is stretching. After exercise the muscles are warm and pliable — this is the optimal time for static stretching, because the muscle fibres lengthen most easily at elevated temperature. Regular post-exercise stretching helps to maintain and improve flexibility over time. It also reduces the sensation of tightness and stiffness that can set in within hours of a training session.

Key Fact

OCR’s two cool-down components: (1) low intensity exercise (gradual reduction in activity) — maintains blood circulation to remove lactic acid and waste products and prevents blood pooling; (2) stretching — maintains and improves flexibility and reduces post-exercise muscle stiffness.

Physical Benefits of Cooling Down

OCR lists eight specific physical benefits of a cool-down. The body’s transition back to a resting state is managed gradually: heart rate lowers progressively rather than abruptly, and body temperature reduces safely. Blood circulation continues so that oxygen is still supplied to muscles during the recovery phase. Breathing rate gradually reduces as metabolic demand falls. Waste products such as lactic acid are removed more effectively when blood flow is maintained — an athlete who stops abruptly cannot clear waste products as efficiently. The risk of muscle soreness and stiffness is reduced: regular cool-down stretching aids recovery by lengthening muscles that have been held in shortened positions during exercise and reducing the severity of post-exercise soreness.

Lactic acid is produced during anaerobic respiration when the oxygen supply cannot meet the energy demand of the muscles. It accumulates in the muscle and bloodstream during intense exercise, contributing to the burning sensation and fatigue associated with high-intensity effort. During the cool-down, maintaining blood flow allows this lactic acid to be transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose through a process called the Cori cycle. Stretching during the cool-down helps realign muscle fibres and reduce the tight, contracted sensation in muscles that have worked hard. Together, these effects mean the performer can return to quality training sooner.
before.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about warm-up or cool-down, avoid simply listing components. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. For example, rather than writing “the pulse raiser raises heart rate,” develop it: “the pulse raiser gradually raises body temperature, which increases muscle pliability and reduces the risk of muscle strains — particularly important for a gymnast whose movements demand maximum hip and shoulder flexibility from the first routine.” For 2-mark “State Two” questions, ensure your two benefits are genuinely different physiological effects — “raises heart rate” and “increases blood flow” are related but distinct enough to earn two marks, whereas “raises heart rate” and “heart rate goes up” will only earn one. Note: OCR names five warm-up components, not four — mobility and dynamic movements are separate stages.

practice_questions.text: Explain why skill rehearsal is included as the final component of a warm-up, and how it differs from the pulse raiser.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 county-level rugby team has 25 minutes before a regional semi-final. Their coach is planning a structured warm-up. Analyse the importance of each component of an effective warm-up for the rugby players before this match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): all five components identified and each clearly linked to a physiological benefit specific to rugby. Pulse raiser: raises body temperature, increases heart rate and blood flow to muscles needed for explosive sprinting and tackling; mobility: loosens joints, particularly the hips, shoulders and neck which are under significant contact pressure in rugby; stretching: increases flexibility of hamstrings and hip flexors needed for sprinting, and shoulders for tackling and lifting; dynamic movements: includes sprint-and-change-of-direction drills replicating the demands of ruck and maul play; skill rehearsal: includes passing, lineout lifting and scrummaging technique rehearsal to prime neuromuscular pathways specific to rugby decision-making. Uses accurate physiological terminology throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): at least three components described with correct benefits; at least two benefits applied to rugby specifically; generally accurate terminology.

Developing (2 marks): two components identified and described; limited sporting application; one or more physiological effects correctly stated.

Emerging (1 mark): names one component or states one general benefit of warming up without development or application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of including both a warm-up and a cool-down in a training programme for a competitive swimmer who trains six days per week.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): evaluates both warm-up and cool-down with a balanced two-sided argument. Warm-up arguments for: raises body temperature (improves muscle pliability and speed of contraction needed for powerful stroke technique); increases blood flow and oxygen to muscles (supports aerobic energy system from the start of a session); mobilises shoulder and hip joints (high importance in swimming); skill rehearsal of stroke technique primes neuromuscular pathways. Warm-up arguments against/limitation: a swimmer training six days per week may find warm-up time cuts into overall session volume; time pressure in competition warm-up lanes. Cool-down arguments for: removes lactic acid accumulated during intense sprint sets; static stretching maintains shoulder flexibility (high relevance given overuse risk in swimmers); reduces muscle soreness, allowing quality training on consecutive days. Cool-down arguments against/limitation: swimmer fatigue and time pressure may reduce compliance; cool-down in cold pool water may be less effective than on land. Reaches a justified conclusion about relative importance, applying to swimming context throughout.

Secure (5–6 marks): both warm-up and cool-down covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to swimming; generally accurate physiological content.

Developing (3–4 marks): one of warm-up or cool-down covered in more depth; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic statements about one component; little application to swimming; descriptive rather than evaluative.

before.exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about injury prevention, the mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sporting application. A common error is listing prevention strategies without explaining how they reduce injury — always link the strategy to the injury mechanism it prevents. For example: “Wearing shin pads in football reduces the risk of tibial fractures and lacerations from direct contact, because the pad absorbs and disperses the impact energy across a larger surface area.” For “Describe” questions about hazards, name the setting, name the specific hazard, and explain why it causes injury. Vague answers such as “the floor could be wet” without naming the setting or injury type will only earn one mark of a possible two or three. For “8-mark Evaluate,” weigh up which strategies are most effective and in which settings — PPE may be critical in contact sport but less relevant in swimming.

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: free weights left on the floor as a trip hazard; incorrect weight machine settings trapping a limb; wet floor near a water fountain; absence of a spotter during heavy lifts; cables or resistance bands positioned at head height. Accept any specific, plausible fitness-centre hazard.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'personal protective equipment' (PPE) and give one example of its use in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition that identifies PPE as equipment worn to protect the body from impact or injury during sport; 1 mark for a correct sporting example (e.g. shin pads in football, a batting helmet in cricket, a mouthguard in rugby, a cycle helmet, knee pads in volleyball). Definition and example must both be present for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two hazards that could cause injury on a playing field, and explain how each hazard could be managed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each of two distinct playing-field hazards (e.g. uneven ground causing ankle sprains; debris such as stones or glass causing cuts or trips; unanchored goalposts causing crush injuries if they fall; waterlogged or frozen ground increasing fall risk) and 1 mark for a correct corresponding management strategy (e.g. pre-match pitch inspection; removing debris before play; checking goalpost anchoring; postponing play in extreme weather). Award 1 mark for a correct hazard with no management strategy if only one hazard is described with its management. Do not award both marks for two versions of the same hazard (e.g. wet grass and slippery pitch).

practice_questions.text: Explain how using a warm-up and cool-down before and after exercise can help prevent injury.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: warm-up raises muscle temperature, making muscles more pliable and reducing the risk of strains during explosive movements (1); warm-up increases the pliability of tendons and ligaments, which are more elastic at higher temperatures (1); cool-down maintains blood flow to remove lactic acid and reduce post-exercise muscle stiffness, reducing the risk of injury in subsequent sessions (1); cool-down stretching helps muscles return to their resting length, reducing tightness that could cause compensatory movement patterns and injury in the next session (1).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school PE department is conducting a risk assessment for a swimming gala to be held in the school pool. Analyse the potential hazards present in this setting and how they could be minimised.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies multiple swimming pool hazards with their injury mechanisms and corresponding management strategies, and analyses why each matters in the context of a school event. Slippery pool surrounds: risk of falls onto hard, non-absorbent surface causing head or limb fractures; managed by ensuring non-slip matting around the pool edge and enforcing a no-running rule. Diving into shallow water: risk of cervical spine fractures and serious head injury; managed by enforcing feet-first entry in shallow areas and clearly marking water depth. Overcrowding: risk of collisions during swimming; managed by using lane ropes and staggered heats. Inadequate supervision: a school gala has many young swimmers; managed by having qualified lifeguards positioned at opposite ends of the pool. Chemical hazards: pool chemicals (chlorine, pH adjustment) are hazardous; managed by ensuring storage areas are locked and only accessible to qualified staff. Demonstrates understanding of the link between hazard, injury mechanism and prevention throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): three or more hazards identified with correct injury mechanisms and management strategies; some analysis of why the measures matter in a school context.

Developing (2 marks): two hazards identified correctly; limited analysis; some management strategies.

Emerging (1 mark): one hazard named with minimal development or management strategy.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of personal protective equipment (PPE) and correct clothing and footwear as methods of preventing injury in sport, considering both their benefits and their limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): provides a balanced evaluation of both PPE and clothing/footwear, with benefits and limitations of each applied to named sporting examples. PPE benefits: absorbs or deflects impact forces that would otherwise cause fractures, lacerations or concussions (e.g. a rugby scrum cap reduces the severity of head impacts; shin pads protect the tibia in football). PPE limitations: can only protect the body part it covers; may limit range of movement or create a false sense of security leading to reckless play; must be correctly fitted to be effective — poorly fitting helmets may actually increase injury risk. Clothing/footwear benefits: sport-specific footwear provides appropriate grip and support (e.g. football boots on grass, swimming goggles protecting eyes from chlorine); compression garments support muscles and reduce strain risk. Clothing/footwear limitations: incorrect footwear in one setting may cause injury in another (e.g. metal studs on artificial turf); clothing cannot prevent all impact injuries and may not be a complete substitute for PPE in contact sports. Concludes with a justified assessment of which is more broadly effective or whether both are necessary. Sporting examples used throughout.

Secure (5–6 marks): both strategies covered with some two-sided argument; sporting application present; generally accurate.

Developing (3–4 marks): at least one strategy covered with some benefit and limitation; limited balance; some sporting context.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic statements about PPE or clothing; minimal sporting application; descriptive rather than evaluative.
